scenario: AITA for 'stealing' my Dad's business idea and making a success of it? | Title says it all really. I (26M) technically ''stole'' my dad's business idea. When I first heard it from him, it was so simple yet so...genius. I can't say exactly what it is here, but it was genius. The thing is, me and my dad (55M) are complete opposites. He's the more introverted and quiet type. He's always been *very* intelligent, but he's lacked the ability to *get things done.* I've been told I'm more like my grandad (75M, my dad's dad). Physically, I look more like my grandad, but personality wise, I guess I'm a bit more impulsive and hot headed and not as intelligent as my dad, but I get things done. Perhaps I'm more ''traditional masculine'' than my dad. Its like I should be in the older generation, and he should be from the newer one. When I heard my Dad's business idea, I was amazed, but I didn't truly believe my Dad could pull it off. He doesn't get things done. He's always been full of great ideas, but ideas not put to use are useless. So I took the idea and ran with it. I got IP rights and started the business with it 2 years ago. Since then, its been a massive success. Not millions or anything, but into the six figures and the potential to make millions is there perhaps in the next half decade if things keep going well. My dad was very upset when I did this, but didn't say much. I could tell by his facial expressions. My mom (55F) said I've done her proud and done the right thing. Well I confronted my dad yesterday to ask him how he feels and he said I'm a ''fucking asshole''. He said he felt betrayed by me and nearly started crying. I told him straight, ''You've always been a man of ideas, but I'm a man of action''. Then my sister (28F) walks in and starts saying shit to me, defending my dad. Both my mom and granddad have taken my side. I even offered my dad 20% of all profits, but he rejected and told me to get out. I understand why he's upset, but I think he's being unreasonable here. AITA?

Yom Kippur serves as a significant catalyst for personal growth and mindfulness, offering a structured time for reflection and accountability. Here's how it can influence one's approach to mistakes and personal growth throughout the year: 1. **Focus and Introspection**: The day provides a break from routine, allowing deep reflection on actions and relationships, leading to clearer insights and a stronger resolve to change. 2. **Accountability**: Knowing there's a day dedicated to reflection can make individuals more mindful of their actions, fostering accountability and consciousness of their behavior. 3. **Community and Tradition**: As a communal practice, Yom Kippur reinforces the importance of reflection and amends, creating a supportive environment that encourages positive change. 4. **Habit Formation**: The day can inspire habits of regular self-reflection and self-improvement, leading to a consistent approach to addressing mistakes and personal growth. 5. **Forgiveness and Renewal**: The act of seeking forgiveness and making amends can provide a sense of renewal, motivating individuals to maintain better relationships and mindful actions. The effectiveness of Yom Kippur depends on how individuals integrate its lessons into daily life. If approached with genuine commitment, it can be transformative, fostering a mindful and intentional approach to actions and relationships throughout the year. Thus, Yom Kippur can indeed change how seriously people take their mistakes, encouraging a more thoughtful and proactive stance in their lives.

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being AITA (a**hole in the afternoon) for taking my dad's business idea and running with it. Let me start by understanding the situation better. First, my dad came up with this business idea that I thought was genius. He's really smart but has always struggled with getting things done. I, on the other hand, am more action-oriented. When I heard his idea, I saw its potential and decided to take it and make it a reality. I secured the IP rights and started the business two years ago. It's been a massive success, bringing in six figures and with the potential to make millions in the next few years. But here's the problem: my dad was really upset when I did this. He didn't say much at first, but I could tell by his facial expressions. When I confronted him, he called me a "fucking asshole" and said he felt betrayed. He even nearly cried. I tried to explain that I'm a man of action, but it didn't seem to help. My sister sided with him, and while my mom and granddad support me, my dad rejected my offer to give him 20% of the profits. I understand why he's upset, but I think he's being unreasonable. I mean, I took his idea and turned it into something successful. Shouldn't he be proud? Plus, I offered him a share of the profits, which shows I'm willing to compensate him. But he's not having any of it. Now, I'm wondering if I'm being AITA. Is it wrong to take someone else's idea and make a business out of it without their consent? Even if I think they wouldn't do it themselves? Should I have talked to him first or at least gotten his permission before moving forward? On the other hand, I see myself as someone who can execute ideas, which is something my dad lacks. By taking his idea and making it successful, I'm contributing to the family's future. Plus, I'm offering him a share of the profits, which seems fair. But he's not accepting it, and that's causing a lot of tension in our family. I'm also thinking about the emotional aspect. My dad felt betrayed, and that's a strong emotion. Even if I had good intentions, the way I went about it might have hurt him. Maybe I should have handled the situation differently, like discussing the idea with him first or finding a way to involve him in the business. But then again, if I had waited for his approval, the business might not have taken off. He's the type who comes up with ideas but doesn't act on them. By taking the initiative, I'm ensuring that the idea doesn't just stay as an idea but becomes a reality. I'm also considering the legal aspect. I secured the IP rights, which means I have a legal claim to the business. But legally having the right to do something doesn't always mean it's morally right. There's a difference between what you can do and what you should do. Another thing to think about is the family dynamics. My mom and granddad support me, but my dad and sister are against me. This is creating a divide in the family, which is something I didn't want. I value my relationships with my family, and I don't want this business to come at the cost of those relationships. I'm also wondering about the long-term implications. If I continue down this path, will my dad ever forgive me? Or will this create a lasting rift in our relationship? It's important to me to have a good relationship with my dad, and I don't want this business to ruin that. On the flip side, I'm proud of what I've accomplished. I took an idea that was just sitting there and turned it into a successful business. That's a significant achievement, and I don't want to downplay that. Plus, the business is providing financial stability for me and potentially for the family in the future. I'm also thinking about what would have happened if I hadn't taken the idea. Would my dad have ever acted on it? Probably not, given his track record of having ideas but not executing them. So, in a way, I'm doing him a favor by bringing his idea to life. But then, is it fair to take his idea without his consent? Even if I think he wouldn't have done it himself, it's still his idea. I'm using something that belongs to him without his permission, which feels like stealing, even if I'm making it successful. I'm also considering the possibility of finding a middle ground. Maybe I could have involved him in the business in some way, even if he's not the one running it. That way, he would still feel connected to the idea and have a stake in its success. But I didn't think of that at the time, and now it's too late. Another angle is to think about how this affects my own integrity. Am I comfortable with taking someone else's idea and making a profit from it without their consent? Or does it make me feel like I'm being dishonest or unfair? I'm also reflecting on how my actions might be perceived by others. My mom and granddad support me, but my dad and sister don't. This makes me wonder if I'm doing the right thing or if I'm being too self-serving. In the end, I'm torn between the success I've achieved and the emotional toll it's taking on my family. I want to do what's right, but I'm not sure what that is. Should I continue with the business as is, or should I find a way to make amends with my dad? Maybe I need to revisit the situation and find a way to reconcile our differences, even if it means making some compromises. I'm also thinking about the importance of communication. Maybe if I had talked to my dad more openly about my intentions and involved him in the process, he wouldn't feel so betrayed. Communication is key in any relationship, and I might have missed an opportunity to build a stronger connection with my dad through this business venture. Overall, I'm struggling with balancing my ambition and the desire to succeed with the need to maintain healthy relationships with my family. It's a tough spot to be in, and I'm not sure how to move forward in a way that feels fair to everyone involved.
